label: Critical mass

construct.source: Marwell, G. and Oliver, P. (1993) The Critical Mass in Collective Action; Oliver, P., Marwell, G. and Teixeira, R. (1985) A theory of the critical mass, American Journal of Sociology
construct.changed: Marwell and Oliver (1993, recalled) describe a critical mass of a few contributors with many resources, whose early contributions make a public good viable for the rest. Here each account could place one pixel per interval, and members in 236 rooms used scripts or spare accounts to place more. Of 11 sampled judgments of the room's hands, 6 named the readership or the canvas, 5 named no ground, and none rested on who answered a call (F-015, weak). No threshold of hands has been tested.
construct.mistaken_for: Olson's free-rider problem, or a tipping point (Granovetter 1978, recalled). The themes here hold calls, explanations of the canvas and judgments of the room's numbers. A read prompted by threshold models found no judgment of numbers that rested on who answered (F-015, weak).
construct.disconfirm_elsewhere: In another setting with a per-person rate limit, groups whose calls, explanations and voiced doubts differ show no difference in whether their work appears.
construct.gloss: We don't have enough people to get it all.

question: Whether a scattered readership gathers enough hands, who know how to place, to make a work viable on the clock; and how a room reads its own numbers.
predicate: A fourth-order theme belongs when its acts bear on the number of hands a room can put on the canvas: calling them, teaching them how, or judging whether there are enough.

label: Coordination without command

construct.changed: Coined, this corpus's. It names the ways members tried to align many hands on one picture when no one could give an order that bound anyone.
construct.mistaken_for: Mintzberg's mutual adjustment (recalled), or self-organization in general. The dimension holds reports of the work's state, templates, scripts, chats and the rare decided order (46 of 705 rooms, F-006). What joins them is that no member could order another to place.
construct.disconfirm_elsewhere: In another setting where many people with no authority over one another make one artefact, the artefact comes out coherent with none of these routes present: no shared design, trace, standard, machine, closed venue or decided order.
construct.gloss: This is the new plan! Everyone do this!

question: How hands that no one can command come to place the same picture: what settles what the room acts on, and what aligns the placing.
predicate: A fourth-order theme belongs when its acts settle what the room will make or align many placers on it: the emblem chosen, the trace read, the template held, the script run, the chat that decides, the leader or vote.

label: Maintenance

construct.source: Graham, S. and Thrift, N. (2007) Out of order: understanding repair and maintenance, Theory, Culture and Society
construct.changed: Graham and Thrift (2007, recalled) describe the routine care of infrastructures by those charged with it. Here no one held authority over another's placing, so care could be asked for or volunteered but not ordered; members in 24 rooms covered a night shift. Members report attacks, and they report changes they later find were a friend's work or their own mistake (46 rooms). Attribution was tested as the step that decides between restraint and attack, and the order test did not find it (a null result).
construct.mistaken_for: Defence, or resilience. Defence is one act inside it; resilience names an outcome, the work surviving, which this study reads from the record and never from the canvas.
construct.disconfirm_elsewhere: In another open, shared surface, works survive as long without anyone watching, repairing or tracing changes as with them.
construct.gloss: The logo is being taken down by others. We need to band together to fix it!

question: What keeps a finished work alive on a surface anyone can change, and how a room decides what a change to its work was.
predicate: A fourth-order theme belongs when its acts keep a placed work as it was, or read a change to it so that the room can respond.

label: Order without law

construct.source: Ellickson, R. C. (1991) Order Without Law: How Neighbors Settle Disputes
construct.changed: Ellickson (1991, recalled) describes neighbours who settle disputes by informal norms, with the law in the background and a long shared future. Here anyone could change any pixel, placement lasted 73 hours, and no room could order its placers to keep a deal. Members in 13 rooms altered other rooms' work as a joke: 'We were busy all game trying to make it say Cocks.' [cardinals/c0065].
construct.mistaken_for: Anarchy in the international-relations sense, or the governance of a commons (Ostrom, recalled). Rooms carrying talk of borders, truces and deals with one other room (467) outnumber rooms carrying bodies of rooms (146).
construct.disconfirm_elsewhere: In another surface shared by groups with no authority over them, neighbouring groups neither claim, spare, bargain, trade help nor federate in recurring forms, and order between them arises by chance.
construct.gloss: We defined our minimized border as per agreement, just draw around the black line.

question: How rooms that share one surface, with no authority over any of them, come to hold, spare, trade, settle and federate over space and help.
predicate: A fourth-order theme belongs when its acts are directed at another room as a party to an order: a claim against it, restraint toward it, a deal, help, or a body of rooms. Moves against a rival and talk with a rival belong to Contention.

label: Collective identity

construct.source: Melucci, A. (1995) The process of collective identity, in Johnston and Klandermans (eds) Social Movements and Culture; Polletta, F. and Jasper, J. M. (2001) Collective identity and social movements, Annual Review of Sociology
construct.changed: Melucci (1995) and Polletta and Jasper (2001), recalled, describe collective identity negotiated inside a movement over time. Here more rooms carry the themes of a membership from before the canvas (Frame bridging, 242 rooms; Flagging the nation, 62) than the theme of factions named for a colour (Neo-tribes, 35). Members also draw a line about what may stand on the canvas (Symbolic boundaries, 49). Membership carried in does not come before the attack more often than chance (F-011).
construct.mistaken_for: Social identity in the psychological sense (Tajfel and Turner, recalled), or the room's emblem. The emblem is what the room chooses to show on the canvas; identity is the membership members claim in the thread, as in 'a fellow comrade during the button' [PurplePixels/c0165], a tie from before the canvas.
construct.disconfirm_elsewhere: In another collective task on a shared surface, groups with a strong prior membership (a nation, a fandom) organize no differently from groups without one, and no group draws lines about what may stand.
construct.gloss: Brothers! Lets draw the Palestinian flag on /r/place!

question: What membership the work carries: who the room is when it places, where that membership comes from, and what it will not let stand.
predicate: A fourth-order theme belongs when its acts express or enforce a membership the room brings to the canvas or forms on it: national, fandom, factional, or a moral line about symbols.

label: Host framing

construct.changed: Coined, this corpus's. It names what a standing community does with a passing event inside its own space: lay a play frame over it, or draw a line around it.
construct.mistaken_for: Goffman's frame analysis (recalled) in general, or gatekeeping. Frame analysis would cover every interpretation in the corpus; this names only the host community's handling of its own space during the event.
construct.disconfirm_elsewhere: In another passing event that arrives inside standing communities, the communities neither play with it nor contain it: the event's talk mixes with their usual business and no one sets its frame.
construct.gloss: Mods really gonna tag jokes as April Fools? Doesn't that kind of ruin it?

question: What the standing community did with the event inside its own space: whether it keyed its space as play, contained the event, or both, and so on whose terms the room's canvas work was talked about.
predicate: A fourth-order theme belongs when its acts set or contest the frame of the host community's own space during the event.

label: Imprinting

construct.source: Stinchcombe, A. L. (1965) Social structure and organizations, in March (ed) Handbook of Organizations; Marquis, C. and Tilcsik, A. (2013) Imprinting: toward a multilevel theory, Academy of Management Annals
construct.changed: Stinchcombe (1965) and Marquis and Tilcsik (2013), recalled, describe how conditions at an organization's founding persist in it. Here members leave marks of the episode in their rooms near its end and after it: celebrations, records, proposed emblems, proposed ties, reported newcomers and, after hour 73, talk about which record of the canvas to keep (P22, tentative). Most rooms existed before the canvas; 78 of 705 have no posts in the week before it. Whether founding conditions set what persisted is not tested.
construct.mistaken_for: Legacy, or organizational memory. Memory is one route; the dimension also holds the return on being seen and what members propose to carry on into later groups.
construct.disconfirm_elsewhere: In another temporary collective episode inside standing communities, the episode's end leaves nothing in them: no marking, record, emblem, tie or newcomer.
construct.gloss: I decided to make some pixel art for a potential banner inspired by our work on /r/place

question: What the episode leaves behind in the standing community: what is marked, recorded, carried on, and brought in by being seen.
predicate: A fourth-order theme belongs when its acts fix, carry or return something of the canvas work into the community beyond the clock.

label: Contention

construct.source: Tilly, C. and Tarrow, S. (2007) Contentious Politics (recalled)
construct.changed: Tilly and Tarrow (2007, recalled) describe contention as claim-making against or through authorities, with a repertoire learned over years. Here rooms contest each other's pixels within the 73 hours of placement. Members in 13 rooms alter another room's work as a joke: 'We were busy all game trying to make it say Cocks.' [cardinals/c0065]. Whether rooms learned their moves from each other is not counted.
construct.mistaken_for: Conflict as the breakdown of order between rooms. Here the contest and the talk that answers it run in the same room: the first attack call comes before the first sparing, refusal or apology in 82 of 104 rooms (A16), and before the first border talk in 95 of 172 (A17); these are orders of first concepts, not proof that each answer met the same call.
construct.disconfirm_elsewhere: On another surface shared by groups, attacks are never answered inside the attacking group by refusal or talk, and are never carried on in talk with the rival.
construct.gloss: It's been a well fought war today : ) I've been trying to fuck up your CLG all day

question: How a room wages a contest with another room and carries it on: the moves against the rival's work, and the talk that makes the rival a party.
predicate: A fourth-order theme belongs when its acts are directed against another room as a rival: moves against its work, or talk that names it as an opponent.
